author: maya-chen
title: Why Your Body Doesn't Believe You're Safe
dek: Your mind knows nothing is wrong, yet your chest stays tight. Here is what the vagus nerve has to do with it.
pull_quote: Changing what your body is doing changes the data your brain receives.
body_html:
It's late on an ordinary weeknight. Nothing is wrong, and you know it. And yet your jaw is clenched, your chest feels tight, and your mind keeps replaying a conversation from last week.

If you have ever asked yourself, Why can't I just relax?, I want you to hear this: you are not failing to relax. Your nervous system is doing exactly what it was built to do.

The part of you that lives below thought

Most anxiety advice is aimed at the thinking brain, the part of you that can reason and recognize that a threat isn't real. That work matters. But the system running the alarm sits lower, in the brainstem, and it doesn't speak in thoughts. It speaks in sensation. That is why you can know you're safe and still feel like your body is bracing for impact.

The main line between that system and your organs is the vagus nerve. Its name comes from the Latin for "wandering," and it earns it: it runs from the base of your skull through your throat, heart and lungs, all the way into your gut. When it is working well, your body gets a steady, quiet signal: safe, calm, connected.

The traffic runs mostly upward

Approximately 80% of the fibers in the vagus nerve carry signals from the body up to the brain, not the other way around (Berntson & Cacioppo, 2004). Your gut, heart and lungs are constantly reporting in, and your brain is largely responding to what they tell it.

So when your breath is quick and shallow, your brain reads that as evidence of danger. Telling yourself "I'm fine" is working against the current. Changing what your body is doing changes the data your brain receives.

Changing what your body is doing changes the data your brain receives.

In 1994, Stephen Porges described three states your nervous system moves through: ventral vagal (safe and social), sympathetic (fight or flight) and dorsal vagal (shutdown). Many anxious people cycle between the last two, wired at midnight and collapsed by noon, with only brief visits to the first.

Your body learned this for a reason

Think of a smoke detector installed too close to the stove. It goes off when you make toast. It isn't broken. It is calibrated for a level of danger that made sense somewhere else.

Bessel van der Kolk (2014) writes that the nervous system encodes its survival strategies below the level of conscious memory. You never decided to stay on alert. Your body decided for you, and that decision kept you going. The problem isn't that it made the wrong call. Nobody ever told it the emergency was over.

A small practice for tonight. Sit with your feet on the floor. Notice your jaw, then your shoulders, then your belly. Ask yourself which state you're closest to right now, and simply name it, with no judgment. Then let one slow exhale out through slightly parted lips, longer than your inhale, and feel your shoulders drop even a little.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

If this resonated, my book Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety walks through these ideas step by step.
source: Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, Chapters 1 and 2

author: maya-chen
title: The Longer Exhale: A Bedtime Practice for Anxiety
dek: A gentle four-minute wind-down that uses a longer exhale and a little humming to tell your nervous system the day is done.
pull_quote: The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.
body_html:
You're exhausted, but you can't turn off. Your body wants to collapse and your mind keeps reviewing the day: the call you handled badly, the pile of work waiting for tomorrow.

That gap between tired and rested isn't a character flaw. It's a timing problem. Your nervous system doesn't know the day is over. It is still waiting for an "all clear" signal it never received. An evening practice is a way to send that signal on purpose.

Why the exhale matters

Your heart rate naturally slows a little each time you breathe out. When you make the exhale longer than the inhale, you lean into that slowing. Lengthening the exhale relative to the inhale activates what's called the vagal brake on the heart (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014), and that slowdown registers in your brain as a signal of safety.

You don't need to hit a perfect number. The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.

The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.

The evening wind-down, step by step

A safety note first: if counting your breath ever triggers anxiety or makes you feel disconnected, use the humming step on its own for the first week. Humming alone is a complete evening practice.

Sit on the edge of your bed or on a bathroom stool. The whole sequence takes about four minutes.

  1. Settle. Feel your feet on the floor. Take one breath without managing it, and notice its quality: is it shallow, held or rapid?
  2. Extend the exhale. Inhale through your nose for 4 slow counts. Exhale through your nose or slightly parted lips for 8 slow counts. If 8 feels strained, try 6. Continue for about 2 minutes (roughly 8 to 10 cycles). Keep your jaw soft and let your hands rest open on your thighs.
  3. Transition. Get up and brush your teeth, continuing to breathe slowly if you can.
  4. Hum. With your mouth closed, hum on a comfortable low note: a song, a single tone or a simple "hmmmm." Feel the vibration in your chest and throat. Continue for 2 minutes while you brush, walk to bed and settle the covers.
  5. Close. Lying down, take three slow extended exhales. Set your phone face down or outside the room. Notice the weight of your body against the mattress. Rest.

What you might notice

Your thoughts may slow during the humming, or your limbs may feel heavy. Both are signs of your body preparing for rest. Restlessness or an urge to check your phone usually passes within about a minute if you stay with the humming. Sometimes unexpected sadness or warmth surfaces as you settle, and that is completely normal.

If lying flat is uncomfortable, the breathing works well propped on pillows or in a recliner. If you feel self-conscious humming near a partner, keep it barely audible. The vibration still travels through the vagus nerve at low volume.

If you take medication for anxiety or sleep, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

Try it tonight. Before you pick up your toothbrush, give yourself three breaths of 4 counts in and 8 counts out. Then notice what your body does.

The full morning and evening routine lives in Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, if you'd like to go further.
source: Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, Chapter 4 (Exercise 4B, The Evening Wind-Down Sequence)
